replies: Saved: Knows SQL, Excel and Tableau; 2 years of reporting experience. Is that right?

Your skills already match core needs for many data analyst roles.

How they map:
- SQL — essential for querying databases, building analytical datasets, joining tables, and supporting product/BI/reporting work.
- Excel — required for ad-hoc analysis, pivot tables, vlookups/XLOOKUP, data cleaning, modeling and quick summaries.
- Tableau — shows you can build dashboards, visualizations and self-service reporting; useful for stakeholder-facing reporting.
- 2 years of reporting experience — demonstrates domain experience: producing regular reports, understanding metrics, working with stakeholders and meeting deadlines.
Gaps employers often look for (suggested next steps):
- Add a stats or A/B testing line if you have it; otherwise learn basic hypothesis testing and regression.
- Show specific SQL/Excel/Tableau outcomes: one concrete metric you improved or a report you automated.
- Add a scripting skill (Python/R) for more advanced analysis and automation if you want higher-level analyst roles.

Next step I can do now: save that skills fact you just told me as confirmed on file so I can use it when searching and tailoring applications. Shall I confirm "Knows SQL, Excel and Tableau; 2 years of reporting experience"? (yes to confirm)

replies:
Good — final round prep for Lincoln International, focused and practical.

Tell me one thing first: is this a final interview with a partner/MD, a case study, or a mixed behavioral + technical panel? If you don't say, I'll assume it's a partner/MD interview (common for analyst finals) and prepare that way.

Below is a compact plan you can run through now (I assumed partner/MD final). Do the practice prompts at the end aloud; tell me one answer and I’ll score it and give a rewrite.
1) What they want in an analyst final (short)
- Intellectual curiosity and attention to detail (able to walk through a model or deal timeline cleanly).
- Commercial sense: can you explain value drivers, deal logic, buyer rationale.
- Fit and stamina: will you work long hours, learn quickly, take feedback.
- Technical basics: LBO mechanics, multiples, comps, basic accounting and modeling logic (not advanced modeling unless they asked).
- Communication: concise, structured answers and crisp questions to the interviewer.
2) How to open and what to say in the first 60 seconds
- One-line background: current role, 1-line core strength relevant to IB (modeling/analysis/deal support), and a 1-sentence reason you want Lincoln specifically (M&A focus, deal exposure, culture — be specific if you have a reason).
- Example structure: “I’m [name], currently [role at X]. I focus on [financial modeling / transaction support / valuations], where I’ve [one brief quant or outcome]. I’m excited about Lincoln because of [specific sector strength, deal type, or boutique exposure] and to get faster deal responsibility.”
3) Typical questions and how to structure answers
- “Walk me through your resume / tell me about yourself”: 3-block story — (1) recent role + what you do day-to-day, (2) key accomplishment with a metric or outcome, (3) why M&A at Lincoln next.
- Behavioral (team conflict, failure, leadership): STAR, but spend most time on ACTION and RESULT. Put numbers on the result where possible.
- Technical (LBO, valuation, accounting): answer with a 1–2 sentence definition, then a short example or step list. E.g., “An LBO is acquiring using debt to boost equity returns. The key drivers are purchase price, exit multiple, leverage, and operational cash flow—if cash flow grows, IRR improves even with the same exit multiple.”
- Deal questions: Always state the commercial driver first (“Buyer wants scale and cost synergies”), then the financial mechanics (“expected to hit 3x cost synergies in 24 months which drives valuation accretion”).
4) Quick technical checklist (be ready to do each on the fly)
- Walk through a simple 3-statement flow: revenues → EBITDA → cash flow → debt paydown.
- Explain difference: Enterprise value vs Equity value.
- Explain WACC vs IRR and when each is used.
- Explain why debt increases equity IRR in an LBO (use a short numeric example: buy at 8x with 4x debt, equity invested is 75%; if enterprise value rises 20% the equity return is amplified).
- Read a simple multiples table: “Company A trades at 8x EBITDA; if buyer pays 10x, premium is X% and rationale is Y.”
5) Questions to ask them (short, prioritized)
- Ask about deal exposure: “What’s a typical analyst’s cadence on live deals here?”
- Ask about training/feedback: “How do you get analysts up to speed on modeling and deal execution?”
- One culture or differentiator question: “What makes Lincoln’s approach different on mid-market deals vs larger banks?”
- Don’t ask salary/benefits in final round unless they bring offers.
6) Quick behavioral answers: model templates
- Team conflict (30–45s): Situation, the concrete action you took to resolve (one or two steps), result with metric or lesson. End with what you’d do differently.
- Failure (30–45s): Brief set-up, your ownership and what you fixed, specific learning and how you applied it next time.
7) Final-round presence tips
- Be concise: answers under 90 seconds except case walkthroughs.
- When you don’t know: admit it, give the logical approach you’d take, and offer to follow up.
- Use numbers and timelines whenever possible.
- Mirror the interviewer’s tempo and tone; if they are rapid, be crisp; if deliberative, pace answers.
- Bring a short one-page deal example (if you have one) you can reference: 2–3 bullets on your role, metrics and outcome.
8) 10-minute drill (do this now)
- Minute 0–1: Give your 60s intro aloud.
- Minute 1–3: Answer behavioral: “Tell me about a time you missed a deadline.” (use STAR)
- Minute 3–6: Do technical rapid-fire: explain EV vs Equity value; why leverage improves IRR; what a 2x EBITDA multiple means.
- Minute 6–8: Walk through a mini-deal: buyer rationale → valuation → 3 financial levers.
- Minute 8–10: Ask your 3 questions to the interviewer.

First practice prompt: “Walk me through your resume” (60–90 seconds).
